The extant continuous Gospel is a Greek narrative whose internal narrator does not identify an author.
In Mark 16:1-8 Mary Magdalene, Mary mother of James, and Salome find the tomb open and hear that Jesus has been raised and will precede disciples and Peter to Galilee.
The earliest recoverable form of Mark ends at 16:8 with fear and silence; it contains an announcement of resurrection and promised Galilee but no narrated appearance of the risen Jesus.
Mark 16:9-20 is an ancient, canonical, and widely received longer ending, but vocabulary, style, content, and manuscript distribution indicate that it is later than the earliest recoverable Gospel.
P45, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Washingtonianus, later Greek manuscripts, lectionaries, and Old Latin, Syriac, Coptic, and other versions preserve an evolving textual history of Mark.
A shorter ending, the longer ending, combinations of endings, and the Freer Logion in Codex Washingtonianus attest ancient discomfort and creative transmission at Mark's close.

No Markan text authorizes coercive conversion, colonial mission, religious violence, abuse, medical neglect, dangerous exorcism, snake handling, poison drinking, prosperity extraction, apocalyptic date-setting, or testing God.
Women act as petitioners, recipients of healing, prophetic exemplars, providers, witnesses to crucifixion and burial, and first recipients of the empty-tomb announcement.
